We agree on check-in points, for example a design review early on and a short weekly update, so problems surface early without micromanagement, and I make clear I am available to help. I remain accountable to my manager and stakeholders for the overall result, so if something goes wrong, I own it publicly; if it goes well, the person gets the credit.

questions.title: Conflicting feedback from two senior engineers
questions.prompt: How would you handle conflicting feedback from two senior engineers?

expectedConcepts.label: Understand each person's reasoning and concern
Bring them together to discuss rather than relaying
Decide based on agreed criteria, with an owner

questions.modelAnswer: First I would make sure I understand each piece of feedback and the reasoning behind it, by asking each of them questions, because the conflict is often about different priorities, such as one optimising for simplicity and the other for future scale. Rather than relaying messages back and forth, I would bring them into the same discussion, a call or a single comment thread, and summarise both positions neutrally. Often they converge once they see each other's reasoning. If they do not, I would ask who owns the decision, usually the tech lead or the code owner, and make sure it is decided against the project's goals, then document it and move on.

questions.title: A blameless postmortem that drives action
questions.prompt: How do you create a blameless postmortem that still drives action?

expectedConcepts.label: Focus on systems and processes, not individual blame
Build an accurate timeline and identify contributing factors
Concrete action items with owners and dates
Follow up and share the learnings

questions.modelAnswer: Blameless does not mean consequence-free; it means we assume people acted reasonably given what they knew, and look for the conditions that made the mistake possible. Instead of "Alex ran the wrong command", we ask why the command was so easy to run against production and why nothing caught it. The postmortem starts with a factual timeline, then identifies contributing factors in tooling, process and monitoring. Its most important output is a short list of concrete action items, each with an owner, a priority and a due date, tracked in the normal backlog rather than in a forgotten document. We review progress on them in later meetings and share the learnings with other teams.

questions.title: Build versus buy
questions.prompt: How would you decide whether to build a feature or buy a managed service?

expectedConcepts.label: Is it core to the business and a differentiator?
Total cost: build, operate and maintain versus price
Fit, lock-in, data and compliance risks
Time to market and team skills

questions.modelAnswer: The first question is whether it is core to what makes our product different. If it is, building can be worth it for control and flexibility; if it is a commodity, such as authentication, email delivery or payments, buying is usually better. Then I compare total cost honestly: building is not only development time but also operating, on-call, security updates and maintenance for years, versus the subscription price, which may grow with usage. I check how well the service fits our requirements, the risks of vendor lock-in, and data protection and compliance. Time to market and whether the team has the expertise also matter. Often the answer is buy now, and revisit if it becomes core.

questions.title: Shipping now versus adding more tests
questions.prompt: How would you choose between shipping now and adding more tests?

expectedConcepts.label: Assess the risk: blast radius and cost of a bug
Test the critical paths before shipping
Use safety nets: flags, gradual rollout, monitoring
Record the testing debt and schedule it

questions.modelAnswer: It depends on what a bug would cost and how quickly we could detect and undo it. For code that handles money, security or data integrity, or that is hard to roll back, such as a database migration, I would not ship without solid tests. For a UI change behind a feature flag, released to a small percentage of users with good monitoring and instant rollback, it can be reasonable to ship with tests covering only the main path. In most cases there is a middle ground: test the critical paths now, use safety nets such as feature flags and canary releases, and record the remaining test work as a ticket with an owner so it actually happens.

questions.title: Accepting technical debt deliberately
questions.prompt: When would you accept technical debt deliberately?

expectedConcepts.label: When speed has real business value, such as validating an idea
When the shortcut is contained and its cost understood
Record it with a plan to repay it

questions.modelAnswer: I would accept it when getting something out quickly has real value that outweighs the future cost: validating a product idea before investing in it properly, meeting a fixed external deadline such as a regulatory date or a major customer launch, or learning what users actually need. It should be deliberate and contained: for example a simple implementation behind a clean interface, so it can be replaced later without touching the rest of the system. I would avoid taking debt in the most critical areas, such as security or data models. And I would record it explicitly, why we took it and what repaying it involves, and agree on when we will revisit it.

questions.title: Fast prototype versus maintainable design
questions.prompt: How would you compare a fast prototype with a maintainable long-term design?

expectedConcepts.label: Purpose: learning and validation versus long-term operation
Prototypes are cheap to change but costly to keep in production
Decide upfront whether it will be thrown away or hardened

questions.modelAnswer: They serve different purposes. A prototype is for learning fast: testing whether users want a feature or whether a technical approach works, so speed matters more than structure, tests or scalability. A long-term design is for operating reliably for years, so it needs clear boundaries, tests, observability and the ability to change safely. The danger is a prototype that quietly becomes production because it worked, and then everyone pays its maintenance cost. So I would decide upfront: is this throwaway? If it succeeds, we either rewrite it properly, using what we learned, or deliberately harden it with tests, monitoring and refactoring before it carries real traffic.

questions.title: Is a cache worth its invalidation complexity?
questions.prompt: How would you decide whether a cache is worth its invalidation complexity?

expectedConcepts.label: Measure: is the data read often and expensive to compute
How stale can the data be, and what happens if it is wrong
Consider simpler alternatives first, such as indexes or query fixes
Account for operational complexity and failure modes

questions.modelAnswer: I start with data: is the data read far more often than it changes, is fetching it actually slow or expensive, and what hit rate could we expect? If the bottleneck could be fixed with an index or a better query, that is usually simpler. Then the key question is staleness: how old can the data be before it matters, and what happens if a user sees a wrong value? A product description cached for five minutes is harmless; an account balance or stock level at checkout may not be. If a time-based expiry is acceptable, caching is cheap. If we need precise invalidation on every write, across several services, the complexity and bug risk are high, and I would only accept that for a large, measured benefit.

questions.title: Balancing cloud cost and reliability
questions.prompt: How would you balance cloud cost against reliability requirements?

expectedConcepts.label: Define reliability targets from business impact
Spend on redundancy where it matters most
Cut waste: rightsizing, autoscaling, reserved capacity
Review regularly with cost and reliability data

questions.modelAnswer: I would start by defining what reliability we actually need, based on what downtime costs the business: a payment system might need 99.99 percent with multi-region failover, while an internal reporting tool may be fine at 99 percent in one zone. Different components can have different tiers, so we spend on redundancy, such as multiple availability zones and replicas, only where outages are expensive. Meanwhile, I would cut waste that adds no reliability: oversized instances, idle environments, unused storage, and stable workloads that could use reserved pricing. Then I would review cost and reliability data together regularly, since both change as the product grows.

questions.title: Which optimisation is worth the effort
questions.prompt: How do you decide which optimization is worth the engineering effort?

expectedConcepts.label: Measure where time or cost actually goes
Estimate the benefit in user or business terms
Compare with effort, risk and added complexity
Prefer the biggest gain per unit of effort; verify afterwards

questions.modelAnswer: I start by measuring, because intuition about performance is often wrong: profiling and metrics show where time or money actually goes, and an optimisation outside the bottleneck has no effect. For each candidate, I estimate the benefit in terms that matter, such as faster checkout for users, which may increase conversion, a lower cloud bill, or meeting a latency SLO, and compare it with the engineering effort, the risk of bugs, and the ongoing complexity it adds. A one-line index that halves a key page's latency is clearly worth it; a month-long rewrite saving two percent of an already cheap service probably is not. I work through the list by value per effort and measure again after each change.

questions.title: A simple algorithm or a faster complex one
questions.prompt: How would you choose between a simple algorithm and a more complex faster one?

expectedConcepts.label: Check real input sizes and performance needs
Simple code is easier to read, test and maintain
Measure; switch only if the simple one is too slow

questions.modelAnswer: I default to the simple algorithm unless there is evidence it is not fast enough. The questions are: how large will the input realistically be, and how often is this code run? A quadratic solution over fifty items in an admin page is fine; the same code over a million items in a hot request path is not. Simpler code is easier to read, review, test and debug, and has fewer edge-case bugs, which is a real cost saving. If measurements show the simple version is a bottleneck, I switch to the faster one, keep the simple implementation as a reference to test against, and document why the complexity is justified.

questions.title: Backward compatibility versus a cleaner API
questions.prompt: How do you weigh backward compatibility against a cleaner API?

expectedConcepts.label: Who depends on it and how costly is breaking them
Evolve compatibly where possible: additive changes
If breaking, version it with migration help and a timeline

questions.modelAnswer: It depends on who depends on the API and what breaking them would cost. For a public API or mobile clients that cannot be forced to update, compatibility usually wins, because a broken integration damages trust and creates support work. For an internal API with two consumers we control, cleaning it up can be cheap. Usually I look for a path that gets both: make additive changes, add the cleaner version alongside the old fields or endpoints, mark the old ones as deprecated, and measure their usage. When a breaking change is truly worth it, I introduce a new version, provide migration guides and tooling, and give a clear timeline before removing the old one.

questions.title: Prioritising security work against features
questions.prompt: How would you prioritize security work against feature delivery?

expectedConcepts.label: Assess risk: likelihood and impact of each issue
Critical vulnerabilities interrupt feature work
Reserve steady capacity for security and build it into features
Explain trade-offs to stakeholders in business terms

questions.modelAnswer: I would not treat it as an either-or. First, I assess each security issue by likelihood and impact: an actively exploitable vulnerability exposing customer data stops feature work immediately, while a low-risk hardening task can be scheduled. For the rest, I would reserve a steady share of capacity, for example a portion of each sprint, for security fixes and dependency updates, so they never pile up. Building security into features from the start, through threat modelling and secure defaults, is far cheaper than fixing it later. When explaining priorities to stakeholders, I translate risk into business terms, such as the cost of a breach, customer trust, or failing a compliance audit.

questions.title: Choosing a product success metric
questions.prompt: How do you choose a metric that represents product success?

expectedConcepts.label: Start from the value the product delivers to users
Choose a measurable metric that moves when users benefit
Add guardrail metrics to avoid gaming or harm

questions.modelAnswer: I start from the value the product should create for users and the business, then look for a measurable behaviour that reflects that value. For a note-taking app, "number of signups" is easy to inflate, but "users who create notes in at least three separate weeks" shows they actually find it useful. Good metrics are tied to user outcomes, measurable reliably, sensitive enough to move when we improve the product, and ideally early indicators of long-term results like retention or revenue. I always pair the main metric with guardrail metrics, such as support tickets, latency or unsubscribe rate, so that improving one number does not quietly harm users elsewhere.
